explanations.explanation: Yes, they cry out to the LORD, and the text says why: Jabin had nine hundred chariots of iron, and he had harshly oppressed them for twenty years (Judges 4:3). Jabin is the king of Canaan, by the way. Twenty years of that, and crying out sounds about right to me. I get nervous when one rolling pin rolls off the counter, so I can't imagine nine hundred iron chariots.

The text says otherwise. The Israelites cried out to the LORD, because Jabin had nine hundred chariots of iron and had harshly oppressed them for twenty years (Judges 4:3). Jabin is the king of Canaan. After twenty years of that, I think anybody would be calling out for help.

explanations.answer: March to Mount Tabor with ten thousand men
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Deborah, the prophetess judging Israel, tells Barak that the LORD commands him: “Go and march to Mount Tabor, taking with you ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun.” (Judges 4:6) Barak is the man she summons. Ten thousand men is a big crowd to herd up a mountain. I can barely get six cookie cutters to line up straight.

explanations.answer: Build an altar at Bethel and wait there
explanations.explanation: Bethel does show up in this story, but only as a landmark. Deborah's palm tree stands between Ramah and Bethel (Judges 4:5). The command to Barak isn't about waiting or building. It's “Go and march to Mount Tabor, taking with you ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun.” (Judges 4:6)

explanations.answer: Send a gift of tribute to Jabin in Hazor
explanations.explanation: Jabin, king of Canaan, reigns in Hazor, so I see where that came from. But the LORD's command doesn't mention any gift. It says to go and march to Mount Tabor with ten thousand men of Naphtali and Zebulun (Judges 4:6). That's a march, not a delivery run.

Right on the money. The LORD says, “And I will draw out Sisera the commander of Jabin’s army, his chariots, and his troops to the River Kishon, and I will deliver him into your hand.” (Judges 4:7) Notice who is doing the delivering. The promise comes from the LORD, and Barak just has to show up and march.

explanations.answer: Send him back home to Hazor
explanations.explanation: That's not the promise. The LORD says He will draw Sisera out to the River Kishon, not send him home. Then comes the part that matters: “I will deliver him into your hand.” (Judges 4:7) Sisera is Jabin's army commander, and he's headed toward Barak, not away.

No teaming up here. The LORD says He will draw Sisera, his chariots and his troops out to the River Kishon, and then, “I will deliver him into your hand.” (Judges 4:7) Sisera is the commander of Jabin's army, and the promise is about him being delivered to Barak. I don't see a handshake anywhere in that verse.

Not quite. Barak says, “If you will go with me, I will go; but if you will not go with me, I will not go.” (Judges 4:8) So he sets a condition, and Deborah has to come along. I think he just wants some company on that road. We've all asked a friend to come with us somewhere.

That's it. Barak says, “If you will go with me, I will go; but if you will not go with me, I will not go.” (Judges 4:8) His answer depends on Deborah coming along. I think he wants some company for the road, and honestly, I get that.

Yes, a woman. Deborah says the LORD “will be selling Sisera into the hand of a woman.” (Judges 4:9) Sisera is the commander of Jabin's army, and the text doesn't name her yet. Keep your eyes open as the story keeps rolling.

I see why a king came to mind, since Jabin is the king of Canaan. But Deborah says the LORD “will be selling Sisera into the hand of a woman.” (Judges 4:9) Sisera is the commander of Jabin's army. It's not a king's hand this time, friend.

Deborah doesn't say servant. She says the LORD “will be selling Sisera into the hand of a woman.” (Judges 4:9) Sisera is Jabin's army commander. The verse doesn't name the woman, so we have to keep reading to meet her.

Not this time. Deborah says, “Arise,” and then the text says, “So Barak came down from Mount Tabor with ten thousand men following him.” (Judges 4:14) He goes down to meet them, and he doesn't stay up on the mountain. When someone asks “Has not the LORD gone before you?” you don't sit and wait.

Right, he doesn't wait. After Deborah says “Arise,” the text says, “So Barak came down from Mount Tabor with ten thousand men following him.” (Judges 4:14) She asks him, “Has not the LORD gone before you?” I think that question gets a man moving. It would get me out of the kitchen too.
True. Sisera “abandoned his chariot and fled on foot.” (Judges 4:15) He commands nine hundred iron chariots, and he leaves with his own two feet. I hope he stretched first, baker.

The text says it plainly: Sisera “abandoned his chariot and fled on foot.” (Judges 4:15) He is the army commander, and he runs without his chariot. I'd love to say I never ran from my own mess, but I've run out of a kitchen or two.

explanations.answer: There was peace between Jabin and Heber
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the text gives. Sisera fled to the tent of Jael, Heber the Kenite's wife, “because there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite.” (Judges 4:17) Sisera is Jabin's army commander. I think he figured a friendly house was a safe place to land.

explanations.answer: Jael was a sister of Sisera's mother
explanations.explanation: The text never says anything like that. It gives a different reason: “there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite.” (Judges 4:17) Jael is Heber's wife, and Sisera is Jabin's army commander. No family tree needed.

explanations.answer: Heber owed Sisera a big favor
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't mention a favor. It says Sisera fled to Jael's tent “because there was peace between Jabin king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite.” (Judges 4:17) Heber is Jael's husband, and Sisera is Jabin's army commander. Peace between the houses is the reason given.

That's what he asks. Sisera says, “Stand at the entrance to the tent, and if anyone comes and asks you, ‘Is there a man here?’ say, ‘No.’” (Judges 4:20) He is the army commander, and he wants to stay hidden. He's asking his host to say there's nobody home.

Hazor is where Jabin reigns, but Sisera doesn't mention it here. He tells Jael, “if anyone comes and asks you, ‘Is there a man here?’ say, ‘No.’” (Judges 4:20) He wants her to say there's nobody inside. He isn't asking her to point anyone anywhere.

He doesn't ask for any waiting. Sisera tells Jael to stand at the entrance, and if anyone asks, “Is there a man here?” she should say, “No.” (Judges 4:20) That's a simple answer to a simple question. Nobody gets put on hold.

explanations.answer: She'll show him the man he's seeking
explanations.explanation: That's what she says. Jael tells Barak, “Come, and I will show you the man you are seeking.” (Judges 4:22) Then he goes in, and Sisera lies dead with a tent peg through his temple. I think this part is heavy, so I'll just say that the LORD's word to Deborah comes true in that tent.

Jael doesn't send Barak away. She says, “Come, and I will show you the man you are seeking.” (Judges 4:22) Then she takes him in, and Sisera is there. This part is heavy, but it matches the word Deborah gave Barak earlier.

explanations.answer: No man came to her tent today
explanations.explanation: That's what Sisera had asked her to say if anyone came asking, but she doesn't say it to Barak. She tells him, “Come, and I will show you the man you are seeking.” (Judges 4:22) Then she leads Barak inside to Sisera. This part is heavy, and the text tells it plainly.

The song actually points the other way. After “Listen, O kings! Give ear, O princes!” it says, “I will sing to the LORD; I will sing praise to the LORD, the God of Israel.” (Judges 5:3) So the kings and princes are being told to listen. The praise goes to the LORD.

Right. The kings and princes are called to listen, and then the singer says, “I will sing to the LORD; I will sing praise to the LORD, the God of Israel.” (Judges 5:3) So the praise goes to the LORD, not to the people in the front row. I'd call that a very good use of a microphone.

explanations.answer: The earth trembles and the mountains quake
explanations.explanation: Yes. When the LORD marched from the land of Edom, “the earth trembled, the heavens poured out rain, and the clouds poured down water.” (Judges 5:4) Then, “The mountains quaked before the LORD, the One of Sinai, before the LORD, the God of Israel.” (Judges 5:5) Even the mountains pay attention when He moves.

explanations.answer: The rivers dry up and the sun stands still
explanations.explanation: That's not in this song. Here the earth trembles, the heavens pour out rain, and the clouds pour down water (Judges 5:4). The mountains quake before the LORD, the God of Israel (Judges 5:5). Nothing dries up and nothing stops in the sky.

explanations.answer: The sea splits and the wind falls silent
explanations.explanation: The song doesn't say that. It says the earth trembled, the heavens poured out rain and the clouds poured down water (Judges 5:4). Then the mountains quaked before the LORD (Judges 5:5). It's a loud picture, so no silent wind.

That's the one. The song says, “When they chose new gods, then war came to their gates.” (Judges 5:8) It puts those two things side by side, and that's the song's own sorrowful look back. I think it's a sober line, and it's a good reminder to keep our hearts with the LORD.
A new king isn't what the song names. It says, “When they chose new gods, then war came to their gates.” (Judges 5:8) The choice was about gods. Kings aren't mentioned in that line.

The song doesn't mention new lands. It says, “When they chose new gods, then war came to their gates.” (Judges 5:8) The thing they chose was gods. The song says what they chose, and lands don't come into it.

Not Sisera. At the watering places, the singers “recount the righteous acts of the LORD, the righteous deeds of His villagers in Israel.” (Judges 5:11) Sisera is the commander of Jabin's army, and his deeds don't make the song. The LORD's do.

Right. The singers at the watering places “recount the righteous acts of the LORD, the righteous deeds of His villagers in Israel.” (Judges 5:11) Sisera, Jabin's army commander, doesn't get a mention there. I think a well is a fine place to tell the good stuff.

Yes. The song says it twice: “In the clans of Reuben there was great indecision.” (Judges 5:15, 16) Reuben is one of Israel's tribes. We've all stared at two options so long that the moment passed. I think that's the human side of the line.

Courage is what the song says about Zebulun and Naphtali, but not Reuben. For Reuben it says, “In the clans of Reuben there was great indecision.” (Judges 5:15) It repeats the line in the next verse. Reuben is one of Israel's tribes.

There's no rejoicing in that line. The song says, “In the clans of Reuben there was great indecision.” (Judges 5:15) It repeats it in verse 16, right after asking why they sat among the sheepfolds. Reuben is one of Israel's tribes.

True. The song says, “Zebulun was a people who risked their lives; Naphtali, too, on the heights of the battlefield.” (Judges 5:18) Those are the two tribes Barak summoned (Judges 4:10). After a list of tribes who stayed back, that's a real shout-out.

The song actually says it. “Zebulun was a people who risked their lives; Naphtali, too, on the heights of the battlefield.” (Judges 5:18) Those are the two tribes Barak summoned (Judges 4:10). They get the praise right after the tribes that stayed back.

That's it. The song says, “From the heavens the stars fought; from their courses they fought against Sisera.” (Judges 5:20) Sisera is Jabin's army commander. The song doesn't explain how the stars fought, so I won't either.

Not in this song. It says, “From the heavens the stars fought; from their courses they fought against Sisera.” (Judges 5:20) Sisera is Jabin's army commander. The song names the stars, so I'll stick with that.
No lions here. The song says, “From the heavens the stars fought; from their courses they fought against Sisera.” (Judges 5:20) Sisera is Jabin's army commander. The help comes from the sky.

explanations.answer: They didn't come to help the LORD
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the song gives. The angel of the LORD says, “Curse Meroz,” and then, “…for they did not come to help the LORD, to help the LORD against the mighty.” (Judges 5:23) The text says nothing more about Meroz. It's a serious line, so I'll leave it right there.

explanations.answer: They bowed down to the Baals
explanations.explanation: The song doesn't say that about Meroz. The angel of the LORD gives the reason: “…for they did not come to help the LORD, to help the LORD against the mighty.” (Judges 5:23) The text says nothing more about Meroz than that.

The song doesn't say that. The angel of the LORD says, “Curse Meroz,” and the reason given is, “…for they did not come to help the LORD, to help the LORD against the mighty.” (Judges 5:23) Sisera is Jabin's army commander. The text gives no more about Meroz.

That's her. “Sisera’s mother looked through the window; she peered through the lattice and lamented: ‘Why is his chariot so long in coming?’” (Judges 5:28) Sisera is Jabin's army commander. I think this moment is heavy, so I'll just say she's still watching the road.

That's not who the song names. Ahab was a king of Israel much later (1 Kings 16:30), and he doesn't appear here. It's “Sisera’s mother” who looks through the window and asks about his chariot (Judges 5:28). Sisera is Jabin's army commander.

That's not who the song names. Saul was Israel's first king (1 Samuel 10:24), and he doesn't appear in this song. It's “Sisera’s mother” at the window, asking why his chariot is so long in coming (Judges 5:28). Sisera is Jabin's army commander.

Yes. She keeps telling herself, “Are they not finding and dividing the spoil…” (Judges 5:30) It's what she expects to hear about her son Sisera's army. This part is heavy, and the song lets it speak for itself.

explanations.answer: He stopped to rest on the way
explanations.explanation: The song doesn't give her that thought. She keeps telling herself, “Are they not finding and dividing the spoil…” (Judges 5:30) That's what she expects of her son Sisera's army. This part is heavy, so I'll stay with the words the song gives.

explanations.answer: The rain has slowed the chariots
explanations.explanation: Rain isn't what she tells herself. The song says, “Are they not finding and dividing the spoil…” (Judges 5:30) That's her answer about her son Sisera's army. This part is heavy, so I'll stay with the words the song gives.
